960.bp: Weather and climate scientists need to understand patterns that repeat—seasonal cycles, lunar tides, annual temperature swings. The real goal is to build math that automatically finds these repeating rhythms in messy real-world sensor data (like temperature recordings) so forecasts can separate the predictable cycles from noise.
960.wh: Raw data is chaotic: each repeating cycle might start at a different moment, or shift slightly year to year. If you try a simple formula like 'linear trend plus sine wave,' you run into a wall—the phase (when the cycle peaks) is ambiguous. Real data from different locations or times also mixes all kinds of noise together, making it hard to know if you found a real rhythm or just noise by luck.

The authors split the problem in two: they first strip out a straight linear trend from the data, then model what's left as a mix of cosines and sines—the building blocks of any periodic pattern. To nail the phase ambiguity, they explicitly let each frequency have its own starting position. For extra flexibility, they also build a deep version where a neural network learns nonlinear shapes layered on top of the sine-cosine basis.
960.ww: Cosines and sines are the most natural language for periodic phenomena—any repeating cycle can be built from them, like mixing primary colors to make any hue. By learning which sine and cosine components matter and with what amplitudes, the model automatically discovers which frequencies (daily, weekly, seasonal) are present. Letting each frequency have its own phase offset cuts through the ambiguity: no two time shifts are indistinguishable anymore.
960.po: On climate data from NOAA (the US weather service), the linear version (FG-Linear) beats trend-only models and deep learning baselines, getting the lowest error. The deep version (FG-Deep) doesn't help on this particular small, regular dataset, showing that the simpler approach wins when data is clean and orderly.

961.bp: Ad platforms sell 'cost-per-click' (OCPC) bidding: you pay when someone clicks your ad, but the real win is a later purchase. The platform tries to predict whether each click will turn into a sale, and charges you accordingly. The goal is a fair, accurate price per sale that keeps both buyers and the platform happy.
961.wh: Here's the catch: after a user clicks, the platform waits days or weeks for a purchase signal to come back. Predictions made on clicks that haven't converted yet are totally blind—you're guessing whether someone will eventually buy when you still haven't seen what they do. Ignore this delay and you'll think every click is worthless (predicting 'no purchase' too often), leading you to bid too low and losing money.
961.ap: The authors borrow survival analysis—a statistical tool from medicine that predicts 'how long until an event happens.' Here, the event is 'customer converts to a purchase.' They build a model that can predict conversion probability even for customers still waiting in the pipeline, using their immediate clicking patterns to estimate the future. They offer two versions: one using multitask survival modeling (learning across many related prediction jobs), and one using Cox survival regression (a simpler statistical standard).
961.ww: Survival analysis was built exactly to handle this: situations where you're waiting for an outcome and don't yet know who succeeds or fails. By modeling the time-to-conversion as a probability curve, you can estimate 'this person is 60% likely to convert in the next 2 weeks' even if they clicked just now and you haven't seen the outcome. This lets you charge fair prices for delayed sales.
961.po: Both versions improved platform revenue in live experiments on real ads. The fix lets bidders accurately price clicks that will convert later, avoiding the bias toward underbidding and ensuring the platform earns what sales are actually worth.

962.bp: Big e-commerce and streaming sites need to show the right product to millions of people. They do this in stages: first, scrape data and decide which items matter; then build a model to score items; finally, serve predictions at query time. Each stage usually ignores the others, even though decisions in stage one ripple through stage three.
962.wh: In real systems, products connect to each other (people who buy socks also buy shoes), relate to user history in subtle ways, and vary wildly by context (seasonal, regional, personal history). Building a data set without capturing these relationships means the model is blind to clues. Training a model without remembering that those relationships exist means it can't learn them. And at query time, you can't adapt to new users or new items instantly.
962.ap: RankGraph-Context is a framework that runs the relationships through all three stages. During data prep, it catches which items and users connect (building a graph of relationships). During training, it feeds those relationships as structured information so the model learns how to use them. At prediction time, it can update itself when a new user arrives or product appears, learning their patterns on the fly without retraining.
962.ww: Graphs naturally encode 'who relates to whom.' If the model knows that socks and shoes are related, it can make better guesses about what a new customer wants. By threading the graph through all stages instead of siloing each one, you build a system that learns from relationships at every step—the opposite of the old 'train in isolation' approach.
962.po: Across production systems, the framework improved results on hard scenarios: new users with no history (cold-start), rare products with few sales (long-tail), and showing variety (cross-surface). It also enabled safe online learning—the system can tweak itself based on live feedback without constant retraining.

963.bp: Facebook needs to suggest friends—people you might know. This is harder than recommending products because friendships are social: they rely on shared communities, proximity to mutual friends, and subtle social norms. The real goal is to help real people find real friends at scale across billions of connections.
963.wh: Facebook's graph of 3 billion users is so large that standard graph learning (like neural networks that walk the graph) is computationally infeasible—you'd need to touch too many machines and memories. Yet simple heuristics that ignore the rich structure of social ties miss many good friend suggestions. You need something that's fast enough for billions but smart enough to use social structure.
963.ap: The authors use a pre-trained language model (like GPT-style models) paired with a feature aggregation trick. For each person, they gather information from their friends-of-friends (second-degree connections), extracting both what the graph structure looks like around them and semantic patterns in profiles/activity. The transformer model then learns to score likely friendships by ingesting this richer context.
963.ww: Language models excel at learning from text and sequences; they're fast even on large scale. By converting graph structure into features the language model can consume (who your friends are, what they do), you get the benefits of social awareness without the computational nightmare of graph neural networks on billions of nodes. The aggregation is a bottleneck you can control, keeping memory in check.
963.po: Live on Facebook, the approach improved friend connections: more users found new friends every day. It scales to billions of users and catches relationships that simple similarity misses because it understands both the local social structure and what kinds of people actually become friends.

964.bp: Recommendation systems have a fairness problem: they show you what they think you want most, narrowing your view. If you like both classical music and pop, but your favorite is classical, the system might show only classical forever, cutting you off from pop entirely. The goal is 'calibration': recommendations should reflect your real distribution of interests, not just your top preference.
964.wh: Most systems optimize for accuracy—showing the item you'll like most. That works if your top interest is all that matters, but humans have a spectrum of interests. Calibration requires the system to spend some recommendations on your secondary interests, which means accepting lower average accuracy. Also, people's tastes change over time; static calibration (one set of interest proportions) breaks when a user's preferences shift.
964.ap: The authors extend calibration to dynamic systems where user preferences evolve. They define calibration that adapts to changing taste distributions and simulate long-term effects: if a system maintains calibration over weeks or months, do users actually benefit? They also run a user study to see what people think of calibrated recommendations in practice.
964.ww: If your interests shift but recommendations stay locked to your old proportions, you'll see stale content. By tracking how preferences change and adjusting the balance of recommendations over time, the system stays aligned with your actual interests. User studies reveal whether calibration actually feels good—not just in theory but in lived experience.
964.po: The research illuminates calibration's real value and limits in dynamic settings. Some users love the diversity; others find non-optimal recommendations annoying. The work pushes beyond static theory to show how calibration plays out as preferences evolve over weeks.

965.bp: Social networks and recommendation graphs grow every day: new users join, new relationships form, old ones fade. You want your learning system to stay sharp as the network changes—learning about the new shape without forgetting what you already knew. The goal is continuous learning that handles growth without collapse.
965.wh: Classic learning algorithms have a deadly flaw: when you feed them new data that looks different from the old data (like a graph with new communities), they catastrophically forget what they learned before—the old patterns evaporate. This is called catastrophic forgetting. Worse, evolving graphs have non-stationary distributions: the patterns that mattered yesterday might not apply today.
965.ap: Instead of tweaking weights and parameters (the standard approach), the authors maximize mutual information—a measure of overlap—between node representations (numerical profiles of each node) at consecutive time steps. If your representation at time T is similar to your representation at time T+1, you've preserved what you knew. By keeping representations stable while learning new relationships, you prevent forgetting.
965.ww: Representations (the learned numbers describing each node) capture what the model has learned. If representations stay similar, the model is preserving its understanding. By explicitly maximizing similarity between consecutive time steps while learning new structures, you balance old knowledge and new information. The mutual information trick is a direct signal: high overlap means retention.
965.po: On real evolving networks, the approach consistently beats standard continual learning algorithms. Nodes keep their learned features stable as the graph grows, meaning the system learns new community structure and relationships without amnesia.

966.bp: When customers shop online, they buy sets of items for their next purchase: grocery trips, clothing hauls, streamer setups. Predicting these 'next baskets' helps retailers stock shelves and recommend bulk discounts. The goal is to anticipate what items will appear together in someone's next shopping trip.
966.wh: Real shopping has quirks that simple models miss. People intentionally add low-value items to hit free-shipping thresholds ('I need two more dollars of stuff to qualify'). Meanwhile, shoppers both repeat past purchases (a predictable pattern) and explore new things (much harder to predict). Existing methods treat repetition and exploration as mixed-up signals they can't untangle.
966.ap: The authors use diffusion models—generative systems that learn by gradually denoising random noise into realistic outputs. They run two denoising processes in parallel, one for spatial patterns (which items go together across categories) and one for temporal patterns (how purchase patterns shift over time). They also use information bottleneck theory—a principle that limits information flow—to force the model to route repetitive signals one way and exploratory signals another, keeping them separate.
966.ww: Diffusion models excel at learning compositional structures (how pieces fit together) by learning to reverse noise corruption. Running two parallel denoising flows lets you model time and space independently. Information bottleneck is a mathematical way to say 'this channel can only carry information about exploration, not repetition,' providing a mechanical separation that lets the model learn cleaner patterns.
966.po: The framework captures threshold-meeting behavior (a real but previously unstudied phenomenon), disentangles repetition from exploration, and improves basket prediction accuracy. It's the first to apply diffusion to this task, unlocking new generative capability.

967.bp: Chatbots and virtual assistants need to stay in character: a helpful assistant should be consistent across all messages, a formal bot should stay formal. Inconsistency erodes trust. The real goal is to detect when a bot contradicts its personality and fix it before users see the mistake.
967.wh: Consistency is slippery to detect. A bot might say 'I'm Jane, tech support' in one message and 'I'm Bob, sales' in another—that's obvious. But what if the bot agrees with the user on Tuesday and disagrees on Wednesday about a topic that should reflect the persona? These indirect contradictions are hard to spot because they don't mention the persona directly.
967.ap: The authors build PersonaKG, a knowledge graph capturing commonsense assumptions about personas—if someone is conservative, they probably value tradition; if they're laid-back, they probably don't stress rules. They construct a dialogue dataset with both explicit contradictions (name changes) and subtle ones (conflicting values). Then they train a two-step model: first recognize inconsistent responses, then rewrite them to align with the persona.
967.ww: Common sense about personality is encoded in the knowledge graph: neighbors in the graph represent related traits and values. By checking if a response aligns with the graph's implications for that persona, you catch subtle contradictions. The rewrite step isn't just deletion—it preserves meaning while twisting it to fit the character.
967.po: On their benchmark dataset, the method improved consistency metrics by 12% automatically (and 10% by human judges). It's the first to address indirect contradictions, moving beyond simple disagreement detection to cultural and value-based consistency.

968.bp: Recommendation models are biased: they overweight popular items and neglect rare ones. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) is a famous statistical trick to correct this bias by reweighting each training example. Many systems use IPS, but do people actually use it correctly?
968.wh: The research question is subtle: does IPS work because it fixes bias (making risk functions unbiased), or does it work for some other reason? If IPS is just a side effect, then using it for bias correction might miss the real mechanism—and might even hurt in some scenarios.
968.ap: The authors analyze what IPS actually does mathematically. They find that under typical assumptions, IPS's benefits come less from unbiased risk and more from accidentally enriching the learned representations (the features the model uses) by forcing multi-task learning. They show experimentally that reweighting can harm performance if not paired with multi-task structure, and that multi-task learning alone often does the job better.
968.ww: IPS reweights examples: rare items get high weight, popular items low weight. This forces the model to pay attention to rare items, implicitly learning richer features for them. But the mechanism isn't bias correction per se—it's feature enrichment through imbalanced training. Multi-task learning (training the model on multiple related prediction jobs) achieves the same enrichment more robustly.
968.po: The paper reveals that IPS can actually hurt if applied naively; it's best paired with multi-task approaches. This rewrites how practitioners should think about bias correction in recommendations: multi-task learning offers a more principled path than reweighting alone.

969.bp: E-commerce search is hard because shoppers type vague queries: 'wireless thing' could mean earbuds, chargers, or routers. Search engines try to expand queries—add related words—to catch more matching products. The goal is to automatically guess what a customer meant and broaden the search without adding noise.
969.wh: Users type short, ambiguous phrases against catalogs of millions of products. Semantic similarity (finding synonyms) misses domain context—'wireless' has different meanings in audio vs. power tools. Few-shot prompting (asking an LLM for synonyms) ignores the actual product catalog and can suggest irrelevant terms. You need to ground expansion in what's actually sellable.
969.ap: REFLEX uses reinforcement learning with a live search engine in the loop. An LLM generates expanded queries, but instead of trusting it, the system tests each expansion against the real product catalog and measures how many relevant items it retrieves. Rewards balance two goals: expanding to items relevant to the original query, and increasing breadth (retrieving diverse products). The LLM is trained on this real-world feedback without requiring labeled training examples.
969.ww: The catalog is the ground truth: if an expansion retrieves relevant products, it's good; if it retrieves junk, it's bad. By closing the loop—testing expansions against real search results—you avoid hallucinations and domain drift. The LLM learns what expansions work in practice, not what similarity scores suggest.
969.po: On a large production dataset, REFLEX beat strong baselines in semantic coverage and retrieval effectiveness. Live A/B testing on real users showed measurable gains in relevance, diversity, and engagement—the system learned what expansions work at scale.

970.bp: Smartphones and smart home devices can't send every prediction to a remote server: privacy rules forbid it, networks disconnect, and latency kills user experience. You need powerful recommendation models running on your device itself. The real goal is to give phone users personalized recommendations instantly, locally, without uploading behavior.
970.wh: Large language models are powerful but huge—often billions of parameters consuming gigabytes of memory. A phone has kilobytes to spare. Shrinking an LLM by 100× while keeping it accurate enough for recommendations is a hard engineering problem. Naive compression often breaks performance.
970.ap: OD-LLM uses two complementary techniques. First, Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)—a mathematical trick that removes redundant patterns from weight matrices, shrinking the model without erasing essential patterns. Second, a tokenization normalization technique that makes tokens (the input units) more compatible with low-rank compression. Third, progressive alignment: after compression, iteratively fine-tune layer by layer to recover lost capability.
970.ww: Weight matrices in neural nets often have redundancy: similar patterns repeat across many parameters. SVD exposes and removes this fat. The tokenization normalization ensures that the simpler representation can still capture the model's intended behavior. Progressive layer-wise refinement recovers capability incrementally, avoiding the cliff where compression suddenly breaks everything.
970.po: On sequential recommendation benchmarks, OD-LLM achieved full-model accuracy with 50-100× fewer parameters, small enough for phones. Users get instant, private, personalized recommendations on their device.

971.bp: Graph neural networks are workhorses for social networks, recommendation graphs, and knowledge bases. They excel when similar nodes connect to similar nodes ('homophily'). But in the real world, nodes often connect across groups—conservative and liberal voters in politics, different music genres in playlists. These 'heterophilic' networks stump traditional graph neural networks.
971.wh: The problem sits at bridge nodes—the few nodes connecting different groups. A bridge node's neighbors are dissimilar (by design), violating the homophily assumption. Existing heterophily-aware models still smooth information across the bridge (averaging neighbor features), blurring the boundaries between groups and confusing the classifier.
971.ap: Bridge Breaking Graph Neural Network (BBGNN) identifies bridges without needing labels: it computes a 'bridge ratio' metric measuring how disparate a node's neighbors are. For genuine bridges, it uses a special aggregation mechanism that avoids over-smoothing—instead of averaging all neighbors equally, it adapts to preserve the differences that bridges intentionally connect.
971.ww: Bridges are structural bottlenecks; their neighbors *should* be different. Standard aggregation treats this diversity as noise and averages it away. By identifying bridges (nodes with high neighbor diversity) and using context-aware aggregation around them, the model respects the graph's real structure instead of forcing false homophily.
971.po: Across benchmark datasets, BBGNN significantly improved classification accuracy on bridge nodes and overall graph performance. It's a targeted fix that restores graph neural network effectiveness on heterophilic networks.

972.bp: Recommending to new users (cold-start) and new products is a core problem. New items have no click history, new users have never interacted. Yet both have textual descriptions and structural connections (category, price range, similar products). The goal is to harness text and graph structure together to make smart guesses without interaction history.
972.wh: Graph neural networks learn from connections but stumble when there are no connections to learn from. Text similarity finds synonyms but ignores graph structure. Neither alone solves cold-start for items you've never seen and users with no past behavior.
972.ap: G-TRAC combines two information sources: text (item descriptions, user profiles) processed by transformers (the engine behind systems like GPT), and graph structure (categories, related products) processed by graph neural networks. By learning alignments between the textual and structural representations—forcing them to agree and complement each other—the model uses both sources of information to represent new items and users.
972.ww: Text and structure encode different knowledge: text captures meaning and nuance, graph structure captures similarity and relationships. By aligning them—making sure representations from both sources point to the same high-level understanding—you combine the strengths. A new product can be represented through both what its description says and where it sits in the product graph.
972.po: Experiments show G-TRAC enhances recommendation quality on cold-start scenarios and generalizes across diverse product types. The dual representation exploits both information sources to handle unseen users and items.

973.bp: Sequential recommendation predicts your next purchase by watching your purchase history. But for brand-new users with no history, the model is blind. Yet you know other things about them: demographics, device, context. The goal is to infer what a new user wants from their attributes, then feed that into a sequential model that normally requires past purchases.
973.wh: Cold-start users break sequential models because there's no sequence to model. Simple workarounds (using demographics or social info) ignore the sequential patterns that make sequential models powerful. You need a way to generate a synthetic sequence that captures new-user preferences, then hand that to a standard sequential recommender.
973.ap: CDMRec uses diffusion modeling (a generative technique that builds samples gradually from noise) to create synthetic preference sequences for new users. First, it constructs a Preference-Dominant Sequence from whatever data is available (demographics, context, user attributes), filtering to the most informative signals. Then causal inference identifies which attributes truly drive behavior. Finally, it runs a diffusion process conditioned on these causal features, generating a realistic behavioral preference sequence.
973.ww: Diffusion models learn to build complex structures from noise; conditioned diffusion lets you steer generation toward specific attributes (gender, age, device). Causal inference cuts through spurious correlations: some attributes correlate with purchases by accident, others drive them. By conditioning only on true drivers, you avoid conflating correlation with causation.
973.po: CDMRec integrates into existing sequential recommenders without modification—it supplies them with generated sequences that work as if they were real. Across three benchmarks, it improved cold-start sequential recommendation and seamlessly pairs with mainstream models.

974.bp: Streaming services (Netflix, Spotify, YouTube) have billions of users and millions of hours of content. They're now experimenting with generative AI—using large language models and image generators to personalize experiences, tag content, and create recommendations. The goal is a forum to share best practices and research findings.
974.wh: Generative AI in streaming is nascent and fragmented: researchers publish papers, companies build proprietary systems, and few exchange learnings. Academic research and production systems rarely talk. Problems at Netflix differ from YouTube, but both could learn from each other. No unified understanding exists of what works and what pitfalls lurk.
974.ap: GenAI4SM is a workshop—a gathering of academics and industry practitioners. Attendees share deployed systems, ongoing research, production insights, and technical challenges. The format encourages cross-pollination: researchers learn what industry actually needs, companies learn what's possible in labs.
974.ww: Workshops accelerate learning by compressing knowledge transfer: a deployed solution that took Netflix 10 people and 6 months might take Spotify only 2 months if the design is shared. Real streaming data and scale constraints differ hugely from benchmarks, and practitioners know these gaps. Researchers bring theoretical depth and generalization insights.
974.po: This is a venue, not a research result—the payoff is the conversations and connections fostered. It positions generative AI in streaming as a coherent research area and builds community around shared problems like personalization at scale, content generation, and responsible deployment.
